assumptions: Customer data tables for audit are customers, users, tenants: customers and users already have record_audit_event calls; tenants is an admin-edited table with no audit call. Chose tenants deliberately to surface a gap, flagged to customer as a decision.
Admin endpoints are those in api_group admin (canonical admin). None of them is tagged admin.
The check_admin_role function is the role check the ask refers to.
Policies are advisory; no blocking intent was stated, so I did not make any blocking.
SOC 2 criteria cc6.1, cc6.2 and cc8.1 are related labels only, recorded as tags, not claims of satisfaction.
confusions: AUTH-002 template scope uses tags:[admin] but the workspace's admin endpoints are grouped by API group, not tagged. Unclear whether the template expects tags to be added first; I changed scope to api_groups, which the skill allows, but the template instruction says to keep its rules.
Recipe 'Record who changed what' says name tables whose changes are audited but gives no guidance for choosing which tables count as customer data; I had to infer from audit_log's own comment.
The skill says 'Fill every need' with workspace names but does not say how to choose a set when the customer's words ('change controls') map to several templates and recipes.

The skill's guidance says never to claim compliance but also says to relate policy to a framework via tags; the difference between tag labels and claims is clear, but a wording example for the statement field would help.

CHG-001 check limits say an anonymous-call workflow test fails until the platform enforces auth; the template still includes test.assertion_required so it may show a permanent finding. Unclear whether to keep it.
wished_for: A recipe for 'SOC 2 change management' and one for 'access review' that says which parts are checkable and which are process.
A way to scope admin endpoints by API group in the AUTH-002 template, or guidance that the template's tag must be added first.
Guidance on choosing customer-data tables from the workspace (e.g. a tag or table naming pattern) so audit scope is not guessed.
A statement example for SOC 2-related policies that describes the control without claiming compliance.
why_confidence: Change controls are partly checkable: audit calls on edits (CHANGE-AUDIT) and audit table protection (RET-001) map well to the workspace's real names. Access control maps to AUTH-010 and AUTH-002. Access reviews and change approvals are not checkable at all, and CHANGE-AUDIT's table set and AUTH-002's group scope are my assumptions. No evaluate was run (forbidden in brief), so all object predictions are unverified. All five files parse with zero rule warnings.
